We do not know how to compute ε(G, ℓ) efficiently, or some other value that could replace it. We solve this by perturbing the edge lengths infinitesimally, as follows. (For unit length edges this is easy by taking ε = 1/2n.) We define a new, composite length ℓ2 for G using 2-tuples. The intuition is that a pair (a, b) ∈ R≥0 × Z represents the real value a + b · δ for an infinitesimal δ > 0. This lexicographic comparison is compatible with the test of whether a + b · δ < a′ + b′ · δ for an infinitesimal δ > 0. context: 5 Subquadratic algorithms for special classes of graphs In this section we provide algorithms to test whether a subgraph is isometric or convex, when the host graph is planar or has small treewidth. The idea is to use the criteria of Lemmas 2 and 6 together with modifications of previous algorithms to compute the classical Wiener index. 5.1 Shortening some edges a bit To test whether H ⊆ G is convex using Lemma 6 we have to shorten the edges of E(G)\E(H) by a small enough amount δ, where 0 < δ ≤ ε(G, ℓ). We do not know how to compute ε(G, ℓ) efficiently, or some other value that could replace it. We solve this by perturbing the edge lengths infinitesimally, as follows. (For unit length edges this is easy by taking ε = 1/2n.) We define a new, composite length ℓ2 for G using 2-tuples. The intuition is that a pair (a, b) ∈ R≥0 × Z represents the real value a + b · δ for an infinitesimal δ > 0. This means that we can compare two lengths (a, b) and (a′ , b′ ) using the lexicographic comparison: (a, b) is smaller than (a′ , b′ ), denoted by (a, b) ≺ ℓ(a′ , b′ ), if and only if a < a′ or if a = a′ and b < b′ . This lexicographic comparison is compatible with the test of whether a + b · δ < a′ + b′ · δ for an infinitesimal δ > 0. To carry the perturbation, we define a new edge length ℓ2 in the following way: ( (ℓ(e), 0) if e ∈ E(H), ∀e ∈ E(G) : ℓ2 (e) = (ℓ(e), −1) if e ∈ E(G) \ E(H). The length of a walk (or path) π is defined as the vector-sum of the the 2-tuples ℓ2 (e) over e ∈ E(π), with multiplicity.
